While the Indian version of the game had snakes outnumbering ladders, the English counterpart was more forgiving as it contained equal numbers of each. [...] In Tamil Nadu the game is called Parama padam and is often played by devotees of Hindu god Vishnu during the Vaikuntha Ekadashi festival in order to stay awake during the night.

gancho: No shogi, o xadrez japonês, a peça capturada troca de lado: quem a tomou pode recolocá-la no tabuleiro como sua. E as peças não têm cor; o dono de cada uma é indicado pela direção para onde a ponta aponta.
explicacao: O shogi e o xadrez ocidental descendem do mesmo jogo indiano, o chaturanga. A regra que mais os separa é a das "peças na mão": em vez de sair do jogo, a peça capturada fica com quem a tomou, que pode, numa jogada futura, soltá-la de volta no tabuleiro. O shogi é o mais antigo jogo da família do xadrez com essa mecânica. Não há registro claro de quando ela surgiu. Especula-se que tenha sido no século XV, e há quem a ligue a um costume da época: samurais mercenários capturados em batalha mudavam de lado. As peças também são diferentes: cada jogador tem 20, planas, em forma de cunha pentagonal, e, exceto o rei, as dos dois lados são idênticas: a ponta virada para o adversário mostra quem as controla. A regra muda tudo. Um bispo, que não anda na horizontal nem na vertical, só alcança metade do tabuleiro, a menos que seja capturado e recolocado. Com o tabuleiro maior e as peças que voltam, a complexidade da árvore de jogadas do shogi é estimada em 10^226, contra 10^123 no xadrez.

fontes.trecho: A distinctive feature of shogi is that after a player has captured an opponent's piece, they retain these as "pieces in hand" (mochigoma), which can be dropped back into the game on a future turn. Shogi was the earliest historical chess-like game with this game mechanic. This drop rule is speculated to have been invented in the 15th century and possibly connected to the practice of 15th-century mercenary samurai switching loyalties when captured in battle. Due to the larger board and the drop rule, modern shogi has a significantly higher game tree complexity than FIDE chess, estimated at approximately 10226 compared to 10123 for chess. [...] Each player has a set of 20 flat wedge-shaped pentagonal pieces of slightly different sizes. Except for the king, opposing pieces are undifferentiated by marking or color. Pieces face forward by having the pointed side of each piece oriented toward the opponent's side – this shows who controls the piece during play. [...] Because they cannot move orthogonally, the players' unpromoted bishops can reach only half the squares of the board, unless one is captured and then dropped. [...] There is no clear record of when drops were introduced, however. [...] While both shogi and chess evolved from the same Indian game of chaturanga, they have significant differences. Shogi's drop rule is perhaps the central mechanic that separates shogi from chess

gancho: Em 1846, no Japão, um rapaz de 17 anos enfrentou no go um mestre de quase cinquenta. Após um lance do jovem, um médico que assistia viu as orelhas do mestre corarem. A partida virou "o jogo das orelhas vermelhas".
explicacao: O rapaz era Honinbo Shusaku, então com nível 4-dan; o adversário, Inoue Genan Inseki, era 8-dan. No primeiro jogo entre eles, Genan deu a Shusaku a vantagem de duas pedras. Vendo que não tinha chance, suspendeu a partida sem terminá-la e propôs outra, sem vantagem, com Shusaku de pretas. Foi essa, jogada em 11 de setembro de 1846, que ficou famosa. Shusaku errou cedo, no lance 25, numa sequência de abertura que só tinha sido registrada 24 anos antes, numa época em que essas sequências eram guardadas como segredo profissional. Depois, porém, fez o lance que dá nome à partida, com efeito em quatro direções ao mesmo tempo: ampliava a área das pretas em cima, socorria quatro pedras pretas embaixo, reduzia a força das brancas à direita e ameaçava invadir a posição delas à esquerda. O médico interpretou o rubor do mestre como sinal de que ele tinha ficado abalado. Shusaku venceu por 2 pontos, e esta é provavelmente a partida mais conhecida dele.

fontes.trecho: The  ear-reddening game (Japanese: 耳赤の一局, Hepburn: mimiaka no ikkyoku) is a game of go of the Edo period of Japan, played on September 11, 1846, between Honinbo Shusaku (black) and Inoue Genan Inseki (white). The game is probably Shusaku's most notable game as it contains the "ear-reddening move"—so named when a doctor who had been watching the game took note of Genan as his ears flushed red when Shusaku played the move, indicating he had become upset. [...] Shusaku was 17 years old and a 4-dan player at the time, while Genan was nearing his fifties and was ranked at 8-dan. The first game they played, Genan allowed Shusaku to play with a two stone handicap. Realizing he had no chance of winning, Genan suspended the game without finishing it, and played another one with Shusaku simply playing black without handicap. Shusaku made a mistake early on in the taisha joseki, but would play well throughout the rest of the game to win by 2 points. [...] The first time this joseki was documented was 24 years earlier, in 1822, and at this time go sequences which were developed were held as trade secrets. Play progressed into the taisha five-way junction, with Shusaku making what is now regarded as a mistake on move 25 [...] Shusaku's move, marked Black 1 in the illustration, had influence in four directions simultaneously. While expanding the Black area at the top, it also brought help to the four triangled black stones on the bottom, reduced White's thickness on the right side, and aimed at erasing or invading white's position on the left side.

gancho: No match de 1997, um lance estranho do Deep Blue teria feito Kasparov ver nele "inteligência superior". Segundo um dos criadores da máquina, foi um bug: sem conseguir escolher, ela jogou um lance válido ao acaso.
explicacao: O lance foi o 44º da primeira partida da revanche, em maio de 1997, que Kasparov acabou vencendo. Quinze anos depois, a história ganhou fama com o livro "O sinal e o ruído", do estatístico Nate Silver, que entrevistou Murray Campbell, um dos três cientistas da IBM que projetaram o Deep Blue. Segundo Campbell, um erro no código fez o programa entrar num laço; para sair dele, a máquina escolheu um lance válido aleatório. "Ele nunca considerou que fosse simplesmente um bug", disse Campbell sobre Kasparov. Entre as partidas, a equipe consertou o defeito. O desempenho de Kasparov caiu na partida seguinte, mas ele nega que tenha sido por ansiedade diante do lance inexplicável. Depois da segunda partida, que perdeu, ele acusou a IBM de trapaça, sugerindo que um grão-mestre humano estaria por trás de um lance. No fim, o Deep Blue venceu o match. Kasparov, que já tinha se gabado de que nunca perderia para uma máquina, disse que às vezes via nos lances dela uma criatividade incomum, que atribuía a intervenção humana; a IBM negou. A versão não é unânime: há relatos que situam o lance perturbador na segunda partida, e não na primeira. Quanto o lance aleatório pesou no resultado é algo que não dá para medir.

fontes.trecho: In the 44th move of the first game of their second match, unknown to Kasparov, a bug in Deep Blue's code led it to enter an unintentional loop, which it exited by taking a randomly selected valid move. Kasparov did not take this possibility into account, and misattributed the seemingly pointless move to "superior intelligence". Subsequently, Kasparov experienced a decline in performance in the following game, though he denies this was due to anxiety in the wake of Deep Blue's inscrutable move. After his loss, Kasparov said that he sometimes saw unusual creativity in the machine's moves [...] suggesting that during the second game, human chess players had intervened on behalf of the machine. IBM denied this, saying the only human intervention occurred between games.

Kasparov won the game in 45 moves. [...] Kasparov eventually resigned, although post-game analysis indicates that he could have held a draw in the final position. After this game Kasparov accused IBM of cheating, by alleging that a grandmaster (presumably a top rival) had been behind a certain move.

fontes.titulo: Did a Computer Bug Help Deep Blue Beat Kasparov? (Wired)
fontes.trecho: In May 1997, an IBM supercomputer known as Deep Blue beat then chess world champion Garry Kasparov, who had once bragged he would never lose to a machine. [...] Fifteen years later, one of Big Blue's designers says the move was the result of a bug in Deep Blue's software. The revelation was published in a book by statistician and New York Times journalist Nate Silver titled The Signal and the Noise [...] For his book, Silver interviewed Murray Campbell, one of the three IBM computer scientists who designed Deep Blue, and Murray told him that the machine was unable to select a move and simply picked one at random. [...] The IBM team did tweak the algorithms between games, but part of what they were doing was fixing the bug that resulted in that unexpected move. [...] "Kasparov had concluded that the counterintuitive play must be a sign of superior intelligence," Campbell told Silver. "He had never considered that it was simply a bug." [...] Either at the end of the first game or the beginning of the second, depending on who's telling the story, the computer made a sacrifice that seemed to hint at its long-term strategy.

gancho: Em 2015, o neozelandês Nigel Richards venceu o mundial de Scrabble em francês, na modalidade clássica, sem falar a língua: estudou o vocabulário francês por cerca de dois meses. Em 2024, fez o mesmo em espanhol.
explicacao: No Scrabble, as peças formam palavras em cruz no tabuleiro, e cada palavra precisa constar do dicionário ou da lista oficial usada no torneio. Richards, nascido em 1967 em Christchurch, já era várias vezes campeão mundial em inglês quando decidiu encarar o francês. No mundial de 2015, na Bélgica, ganhou 14 das 17 partidas preliminares e venceu a final por duas partidas a uma. Na modalidade "duplicada", popular entre os francófonos, em que todos jogam com as mesmas letras no mesmo tabuleiro, ficou em segundo, a um ponto do vencedor. Voltou a ganhar o título em 2018. Por volta de 2023, começou a estudar a lista de palavras do espanhol, outra língua que não fala. No primeiro mundial em espanhol de que participou, em 2024, venceu 23 de 24 partidas na modalidade clássica e, na duplicada, em que ficou em segundo, fez as duas primeiras pontuações perfeitas já registradas no campeonato. Richards tem fama de memória e habilidade matemática excepcionais e de ser recluso: quase nunca dá entrevistas.

fontes.trecho: In 2015, despite not speaking French, Richards won the French World Scrabble Championships, after reportedly spending nine weeks studying the French dictionary. He won it again in 2018 [...] In 2024, Richards accomplished a similar feat by winning the Spanish-language World Championships. Renowned for his eidetic and mathematical abilities, Richards has been described as a reclusive person and has rarely been interviewed. [...] Richards was born in 1967 in Christchurch, New Zealand. [...] On 20 July, Richards won the nonduplicate portion of the 2015 French World Scrabble Championship in Belgium after two months of studying the French lexicon. He does not speak French. He won 14 of the preliminary 17 games before defeating the 2014 runner-up Schélick Ilagou Rekawe in the final, two games to one. In the duplicate (rarely played in English, but played in French since 1972) he finished second, just one point behind the winner [...] Richards won his fifth World Championship [...] Around 2023, he began studying the Spanish Scrabble word list and in 2024 competed in the Spanish World Scrabble Championship for the first time. Despite not speaking Spanish, he finished 2nd in the Duplicate format, while compiling the first two perfect scores ever recorded at the championship, and won 23 of 24 games to win the Classic format championship.

The tiles must form words that, in crossword fashion, read left to right in rows or downward in columns and are included in a standard dictionary or lexicon. [...] Duplicate Scrabble is a popular variant in French speaking countries. Every player has the same letters on the same board

gancho: Em 1961, sem computador à mão, um pesquisador montou com 304 caixas de fósforo e contas coloridas uma máquina que aprendia jogo da velha. A cada vitória, ganhava contas; a cada derrota, perdia as dos lances que jogou.
explicacao: O pesquisador era Donald Michie, que na Segunda Guerra tinha trabalhado na equipe que decifrava o código alemão Tunny. A máquina se chamava MENACE. Cada caixa correspondia a uma configuração do tabuleiro; descartando as que eram só rotações ou espelhos de outras, bastavam 304. Dentro, contas de cores diferentes representavam as casas livres. Para saber a jogada, sacudia-se a gaveta da caixa certa, e a conta que caía na ponta de um "V" de cartolina indicava a casa. No começo, as escolhas eram ao acaso. Ao fim de cada partida vinha o "prêmio" ou o "castigo": se a máquina vencesse, as contas usadas voltavam com mais três da mesma cor; se perdesse, elas ficavam de fora; no empate, cada caixa usada ganhava uma conta. Assim, lances ruins iam sumindo. É uma das primeiras versões do aprendizado por reforço. Num torneio em 1961, Michie jogou com a estratégia ótima, e depois de vinte partidas os dois passaram a empatar de forma consistente, que é o que acontece quando os dois lados jogam a estratégia perfeita.

fontes.titulo: Matchbox Educable Noughts and Crosses Engine
fontes.trecho: was a mechanical computer made from 304 matchboxes designed and built by artificial intelligence researcher Donald Michie and his colleague Roger Chambers, in 1961. It was designed to play human opponents in games of noughts and crosses (tic-tac-toe) by returning a move for any given state of play and to refine its strategy through reinforcement learning. [...] Michie and Chambers did not have immediate access to a computer; they worked around this by building the engine out of matchboxes. The matchboxes they used each represented a single possible layout of a noughts and crosses grid. When the computer first played, it would randomly choose moves based on the current layout. [...] Donald Michie (1923–2007) had been on the team decrypting the German Tunny Code during World War II. [...] This was one of the earliest versions of the Reinforcement Loop [...] After removing duplicate arrangements (ones that were simply rotations or mirror images of other configurations), MENACE used 304 permutations in its chart and thus that many matchboxes. Each individual matchbox tray contained a collection of coloured beads. Each colour represented a move on a square on the game grid [...] The tray would be removed and lightly shaken so as to move the beads around. Then, the bead that had rolled into the point of the "V" shape at the front of the tray was the move MENACE had chosen to make. [...] Michie described his reinforcement system with "reward" and "punishment". [...] These were returned to their respective trays, easily identifiable since they were slightly open, as well as three bonus beads of the same colour. [...] If it lost, the removed beads were not returned, "punishing" MENACE [...] If the game was a draw, one additional bead was added to each box. [...] However, if both players use this strategy, the game always ends in a draw. [...] In Donald Michie's official tournament against MENACE in 1961 he used optimal strategy, and he and the computer began to draw consistently after twenty games.

gancho: Em 1964, um antiquário de Edimburgo pagou 5 libras por uma peça de xadrez de marfim de morsa e a guardou numa gaveta. Em 2019, a Sotheby's a atribuiu à oficina das famosas peças de Lewis e a vendeu por £735.000.
explicacao: As peças de Lewis foram achadas em 1831 na ilha de Lewis, nas Hébridas Exteriores da Escócia. Foram provavelmente feitas entre 1150 e 1200, quase todas de marfim de morsa, e a hipótese mais aceita é que vieram de Trondheim, na Noruega. Têm expressões que hoje parecem cômicas, e quatro das torres são guerreiros berserkers mordendo o escudo de fúria. Desde a descoberta, faltavam um cavalo e quatro torres para completar os quatro conjuntos. O Museu Britânico ficou com 82 peças, pelas quais pagou 80 guinéus. A peça de 1964, registrada no livro de estoque do antiquário como "guerreiro de xadrez de presa de morsa antiga", passou de geração em geração sem que ninguém soubesse o que era. Os netos a levaram à Sotheby's, que levou um ano para autenticá-la. Para a casa de leilões, era provavelmente uma das torres que faltavam, em forma de guarda armado, embora a própria Sotheby's admita que o tema segue em debate e a datação por carbono-14 da peça tenha dado uma data mais tardia que a do conjunto. Em julho de 2019, foi arrematada por um comprador anônimo, num recorde para uma peça de xadrez medieval em leilão. Outras quatro peças principais continuam desaparecidas.

fontes.trecho: are a group of distinctive 12th-century chess pieces, along with other game pieces, most of which are carved from walrus ivory. Discovered in 1831 on the Isle of Lewis in the Outer Hebrides of Scotland [...] A newly identified piece, a "warder", the equivalent of a rook, was sold for £735,000 in July 2019. Four other major pieces, and many pawns, remain missing from the chess sets. [...] The Lewis chessmen were probably made between 1150 and 1200 AD. They are commonly believed to have been made in Trondheim, Norway [...] four of the rooks are shown as wild-eyed berserkers biting their shields with battle fury. [...] Scholars have observed that, to the modern eye, the figural pieces, with their bulging eyes and glum expressions, have a distinctly comic character. [...] The museum paid 80 guineas (equivalent to £8,131 in 2025) for the 82 pieces. [...] When the chessmen were uncovered in 1831, 1 knight and 4 warders were missing from the four sets. [...] This so-called "Antique Walrus Tusk Warrior Chessman" was purchased at a Sotheby's auction for £735,000 the following month, by an undisclosed buyer.

fontes.titulo: Attributed to the Lewis Chessmen workshop, probably Trondheim (Sotheby's)
fontes.trecho: 1964, purchased for £5 by an antiques dealer in Edinburgh, recorded in the stock book for that year as ‘Antique Walrus tusk warrior chessman’; thence by descent to the present owners [...] ATTRIBUTED TO THE LEWIS CHESSMEN WORKSHOP, PROBABLY NORWEGIAN, TRONDHEIM, 13TH CENTURY | A WARDER [...] It is a logical deduction that the present warder could be one of the lost pieces from the Lewis group. However, it should be recognised that in the absence of a recorded find site for the Lewis hoard and for the present warder, there is and will continue to be healthy scholarly debate on this subject. [...] The radiocarbon dating for the present warder below indicates a date later than is generally accepted on stylistic grounds for the Lewis [...] There is no comparative Radiocarbon dating analysis (C14) for any of the Lewis chessmen in the British Museum or National Museum of Scotland.

fontes.titulo: Lost Lewis Chessmen piece bought for £5 sells for £735,000 (The Irish Times)
fontes.trecho: Antiques dealer acquired rare artefact in 1964 and was mostly kept in a drawer [...] The piece, bought for £5 in 1964 by an antiques dealer and passed down through their family, has hit a new record for a medieval chess piece at auction, Sotheby’s in London has said. [...] The antiques dealer, from Edinburgh, had no idea of the significance of the piece, which was passed down through the family and mostly kept hidden away in a drawer.

fontes.titulo: Lewis Chessmen Piece Could Go For $1 Million At Upcoming Auction (NPR)
fontes.trecho: It's passed down in the family and was brought to us by the antiques dealer's grandchildren. [...] It took a year for Sotheby's to authenticate it.
